title: Olympic Trap and Skeet, and the road to a world sport
summary: A short look at the Olympic disciplines Trap and Skeet, and at how clay shooting became international: federations, championships, video and online results.

body.html: Besides Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting there are two Olympic clay disciplines: Olympic Trap and Skeet. They are governed by the ISSF, not by FITASC. Their rules are their own, and a shooter used to sporting will notice that everything, from the targets to the pace, feels different.

In Olympic Trap, also called Olympic trench, the targets fly away from the shooter at changing angles. They come out of a trench in front: a long pit in the ground where the throwing machines are hidden. Trap was first held at the 1900 Olympic Games in Paris. It then came and went, and it has been on the programme of all Games since 1952.

Skeet was created in the USA in the 1920s by hunters who wanted to practise shots from many angles. Its name was chosen in 1926 through a readers' contest in two magazines. Today the targets cross the field from two small huts called houses, which hold the throwing machines: a high house and a low house.

Skeet first appeared at the Olympic Games in 1968, in Mexico City. From 1968 to 1992 women could enter the Olympic clay events together with men. The first separate women's clay event was Double Trap, held from 1996 to 2004. Separate women's Trap and Skeet have been on the programme since 2000, and mixed team events came later.

For many people the Olympics are their first look at clay shooting. But other things made the sport international too. National federations joined international ones, and World and European Championships appeared.
Later came Grand Prix events and open competitions that draw shooters from abroad. Today Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting are shot on several continents.

In recent decades the internet added one more step. Results, videos and rankings are online, so you can follow the season worldwide. ClayArena collects this information for Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting: What ClayArena is. ClayAway, a service for training trips abroad, is being prepared.

key_points.html: Olympic Trap and Skeet are governed by the ISSF.
Trap was first at the 1900 Games and has been at all Games since 1952.
Skeet began in the USA in the 1920s and has been Olympic since 1968.
Separate women's Trap and Skeet since 2000; mixed team events came later.
Federations, championships and now the internet made the sport international.

did_you_know.html: Skeet began with one trap and stations in a full circle, like a clock face. When a neighbour opened a chicken farm next to the field, a second trap was placed opposite the first. The shooter got the same angles, but the danger area was halved.

quiz.q: Who governs Olympic Trap and Skeet?
quiz.explain: The Olympic clay disciplines are governed by the ISSF; FITASC governs Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

quiz.q: When did Skeet first appear at the Olympic Games?
quiz.explain: Skeet made its Olympic debut in 1968 in Mexico City.

quiz.q: Since when have women had their own Olympic Trap and Skeet events?
quiz.explain: Women's Trap and Skeet were added in 2000 (women's Double Trap was held from 1996 to 2004). Before that, from 1968 to 1992, women could shoot in the same events as men.
